name: San Francisco del Mar Huave
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.

new_statements.quote: Throughout all examples in the paper, stress is uniformly final. San Francisco del Mar Huave has the following phonemic inventory as described in Kim (2008). [p. 1006] || Fossilized forms found in toponyms are another potential source of evidence, for example [Sume"hama], with penultimate stress, glossed by speakers as referring to a lizard, which in the modern variety is [ham]. [fn. 7, p. 1009] || The acute accent [´] marks high tone, and the grave accent [`] low tone; the tonal contrast has been lost in the San Francisco variety but is reproduced from Suárez's examples for the sake of fidelity. [fn. 6, p. 1008] || Aspirated vowels correspond to nuclei in other Huave varieties that alternate between aspirated vowels and long vowels depending on stress (Suárez 1975). [fn. 10, p. 1015]

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress (fixed final) matches 'stress is uniformly final'. The paper adds that the San Francisco variety has lost the tonal contrast and notes one fossilized penultimate-stress toponym; it defers the full phonological description to Kim (2008), which is already held by the project in this folder.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable in every example (the paper does not give a dedicated stress section; it states final stress as background, citing Kim 2008 for the full phonology). The only non-final stress mentioned is a fossilized toponym with penultimate stress. The proto-Huave tonal contrast reconstructed by Suárez is lost in the San Francisco variety.
new_statements.exceptions: One fossilized toponym [Sume"hama] 'lizard (place name)' with penultimate stress (fn. 7, p. 1009), treated as a relic, not a synchronic pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: The article describes San Francisco del Mar Huave specifically (fieldwork 2004-2013 in San Francisco del Mar, Oaxaca; 'isolate: Mexico'), i.e. the sanf1258 variety, and contrasts it with other Huave varieties (San Mateo del Mar per Suárez 1975 / Noyer) only in footnotes on vowel length/aspiration and tone.

tone_statements.citation: Kim, Yuni (2005). Topics in the Phonology and Morphology of San Francisco del Mar Huave. Berkeley: University of California.
tone_statements.quote: To be more specific, the San Francisco del Mar dialect has no lexical tonal contrast of the (marginal) kind found in the dialect of San Mateo del Mar (Pike & Warkentin 1961, Noyer 1991, Evanini 2007), and there is fixed final stress. There is not as of this writing a sufficient case for secondary stress, syllable weight distinctions, or other complexities in the metrical phonology, though see §2.5.4 for hints in that direction. [...] Primary stress falls on the final syllable of each word regardless of morphological constituency. Stress will therefore fall on the root if there are no suffixes, and on the final suffix if there are suffixes. Phonetically, stress is cued by pitch, with isolation forms typically having a low plateau in the non-final syllables and a high peak in the final syllable (cf. Evanini 2007). It is likely that there are durational differences between stressed and unstressed syllables, although no solid claims can be made until instrumental work is undertaken.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final' rests on the only full description of the variety (Kim 2008 Berkeley dissertation, 371 pp, Glottolog's top 'grammar' entry), which states fixed final primary stress with no secondary stress or weight; quotation verified verbatim at sec. 2.1.5 pp. 35-36 in the PDF downloaded now, and independently restated in Kim 2015. No competing or instrumental study of this variety exists (instrumental work is on San Mateo del Mar, a separate glottocode). Only housekeeping needed: the record's top-level quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank (quotation sits only in sources[0]) and no file was. populate loc='sec. 2.1.5, pp. 35-36', point to the now-held PDF, and set an strength of the evidence. One caveat worth a note, not a reclassify: p.71 scopes the generalization to 'native words' (Spanish loans may differ).
